title: Full overhead schematic of Trumbull-Cliffs Blast Furnace
description:
Longitudinal (overhead) schematic of the Trumbull-Cliffs Blast Furnace in Warren, Ohio, in the United States in 1921.
The boiler house is at left, where steam for the power plant is generated. To its right is the gas cleaning plant, where smoke and fumes are processed. Useable gases are removed, useful liquids are condensed, and smoke filtered out. The hot air is then returned to the stoves ("regenerated").
The stoves pre-heat and re-heat air. This air is then pumped into the blast furnace, where it mixes with the molten iron and causes a "blast" (burning off of oxygen and impurities).
The blast furnace is fed from the top (the "throat"). Iron ore and coke (coal which has been distilled to remove impurities and gases) is poured into the furnace, where it lies atop semi-molten and molten material below. The coke burns, driving off most of the oxygen and some impurities in the ore. As the ore melts, it sinks to the bottom of the blast furnace and collects in the "hearth".
The skip hoist feeds the blast furnace. Skips (buckets) collect ore and coke from the stock bins (far right), and lift it up to the throat.
Slag (molten impurities) float atop the molten steel. Slag is tapped from the top of the hearth, and drawn off by the slag runner. Slag collects in the granulating pit, where it cools and is crushed. (Slag is a useful byproduct.)
Molten iron is tapped from the bottom of the hearth. Iron runners take the material to "ladles", huge rail cars capable of handling the molten material. The ladles then follow the hot metal track to the casting mill, where pig iron is cast in ingots and billets.
The smelter made pig iron. The Trumbull-Cliffs Furnace Company was jointly founded and owned by Trumbull Steel of Warren, Ohio, and the Cleveland-Cliffs Iron Company of Cleveland, Ohio. The firm was organized in Ohio in May 1920.
The blast furnace was erected on the shores of the Mahoning River in Warren, directly opposite the Trumbull Steel plant. Its purpose was to smelt pig iron for Trumbull Steel. It used iron ore provided by mines owned or controlled by Trumbull Steel or Cleveland-Cliffs Iron.
The foundation was first laid on August 14, 1920, and the blast furnace completed on June 14, 1921.
The main stack was 92 feet high, had a bosh which was 22 feet 6 inches feet in diameter, and a hearth which was 15 feet 6 inches in diameter. It had a capacity to make 600 tons of pig iron, making it about 20 percent larger than the average blast furnace in the United States at the time.
It cost $3.25 million to build (in 1920 dollars).
The red-hot pig iron was conveyed via a "hot metal bridge" from the furnace to the Trumbull Steel mill across the river. Congress adopted legislation permitting construction of this bridge.

The blast furnace also had a plant that made coke (a fuel made of distilled coal).
author: "New 600-Ton Blast Furnace Plant". The Blast Furnace & Steel Plant, October 1921, p. 592
